plain_english: Let virtue lead the way and carry the flag. We'll still have pleasures, but we'll be in charge of them. Pleasure might win a few small battles with us, but it won't force us to do anything. But people who let pleasure take the lead? They end up with neither virtue nor pleasure. They lose virtue completely. And they don't really possess pleasure — pleasure possesses them. They're tortured when they can't get it, and choked when they have too much. They're miserable when pleasure leaves them, and even more miserable when it overwhelms them. They're like ships caught in the dangerous shoals of the Syrtes — sometimes stranded on dry sand, sometimes tossed around by crashing waves.
original_excerpt: Let virtue lead the way and bear the standard: we shall have pleasure for all that, but we shall be her masters and controllers; she may win some concessions from us, but will not force us to do anything. On the contrary, those who have permitted pleasure to lead the van, have neither one nor the other: for they lose virtue altogether, and yet they do not possess pleasure, but are possessed by it, and are either tortured by its absence or choked by its excess, being wretched if deserted by it, and yet more wretched if overwhelmed by it, like those who are caught in the shoals of the Syrtes and at one time are left on dry ground and at another tossed on the flowing waves.

plain_english: This happens because people lack self-control and secretly love what's bad for them. It's dangerous when someone who chases evil instead of good actually gets what they want. Think about hunting wild animals — it's hard and risky work, and even after you catch them, they're nothing but trouble. They often attack their own keepers. That's exactly what great pleasures are like. They turn into great evils and make prisoners of their owners. The more pleasures you have, and the bigger they are, the more you become a slave with many masters. Yet ordinary people call this person happy.
original_excerpt: This arises from an exaggerated want of self-control, and a hidden love of evil: for it is dangerous for one who seeks after evil instead of good to attain his object. As we hunt wild beasts with toil and peril, and even when they are caught find them an anxious possession, for they often tear their keepers to pieces, even so are great pleasures: they turn out to be great evils and take their owners prisoner. The more numerous and the greater they are, the more inferior and the slave of more masters does that man become whom the vulgar call a happy man.

plain_english: Let me push this comparison even further. Think of a hunter tracking wild animals to their hiding places. He values highly "catching wandering beasts with snares" and "making his hounds surround the wide clearing" so he can follow their tracks. But while he does this, he ignores far better things and leaves many important duties undone. In the same way, someone who chases pleasure puts everything else second to it. He ignores the most essential thing — his freedom — and sacrifices it to his appetites. He doesn't buy pleasure for himself. He sells himself to pleasure.
original_excerpt:
I may even press this analogy further: as the man who tracks wild animals to their lairs, and who sets great store on—

"Seeking with snares the wandering brutes to noose,"

and

"Making their hounds the spacious glade surround,"

that he may follow their tracks, neglects far more desirable things, and leaves many duties unfulfilled, so he who pursues pleasure postpones everything to it, disregards that first essential, liberty, and sacrifices it to his belly; nor does he buy pleasure for himself, but sells himself to pleasure.
